## What you'll learn

- How **over-representation analysis** (ORA) tests whether a pathway has more responding genes than expected by chance.
- How **gene set enrichment analysis** (GSEA) does the same without a significance cut-off.
- How to look up interactions between genes in STRING.

## The data

Part 3 found hundreds of genes that respond to LPS in each strain. A list of locus tags isn't very informative, so we ask: **are some functions over-represented among them?** We use the KEGG pathways of each gene, and focus on *Bacteroides caecimuris* **I48**.

To save you from running DESeq2 again, `de_i48.csv.gz` has the Part 3 results for I48, computed with exactly the same method.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())

genes <- read_csv("data/genes.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
de <- read_csv("data/de_i48.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
pathway_names <- read_csv("data/kegg_pathways.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# genes that were tested (padj is NA for genes DESeq2 filtered out, see Part 3)
i48 <- de %>%
  filter(!is.na(padj)) %>%
  left_join(select(genes, locus_tag, pathways), by = "locus_tag")

# one row per gene and pathway
pathway_genes <- i48 %>%
  filter(!is.na(pathways)) %>%
  separate_rows(pathways, sep = ";") %>%
  distinct(pathway = pathways, locus_tag)

cat(nrow(i48), "I48 genes tested;", n_distinct(pathway_genes$locus_tag),
    "of them are in at least one KEGG pathway\n")
```

Only about a quarter of the genes are in a KEGG pathway. Enrichment can only say something about those, so they are our **universe**: the genes that could have been picked.

```{webr}
universe <- unique(pathway_genes$locus_tag)
down <- i48 %>% filter(padj < 0.01, log2FoldChange < -1) %>% pull(locus_tag) %>% intersect(universe)
up <- i48 %>% filter(padj < 0.01, log2FoldChange > 1) %>% pull(locus_tag) %>% intersect(universe)
cat(length(universe), "genes in the universe;", length(down), "down and", length(up), "up in LPS mice\n")
```

## Over-representation analysis

Take one pathway, e.g. **valine, leucine and isoleucine biosynthesis** (ko00290). Sort the universe into a 2 × 2 table:

| | In the pathway | Not in the pathway |
|---|---|---|
| **Down in LPS** | *a* | *b* |
| **Not down** | *c* | *d* |

If the pathway had nothing to do with the response, its share of down genes would be about the same as everyone else's. The **hypergeometric test** (equivalently, a one-sided Fisher's exact test) gives the probability of seeing at least *a* pathway genes among the down genes by chance.

### Exercise: test one pathway

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_ora
bcaa <- pathway_genes %>% filter(pathway == "ko00290") %>% pull(locus_tag)

hits <- sum(______)   # pathway genes that are down

# P(at least `hits` pathway genes among the down genes, drawn at random from the universe)
p <- phyper(hits - 1, length(bcaa), length(universe) - length(bcaa), length(down),
            lower.tail = FALSE)
cat(hits, "of", length(bcaa), "pathway genes are down; expected by chance:",
    round(length(bcaa) * length(down) / length(universe), 1), "; p =", signif(p, 2), "\n")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_ora"}
`bcaa %in% down` is `TRUE` for every pathway gene that is also in the `down` list.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_ora"}
```r
bcaa <- pathway_genes %>% filter(pathway == "ko00290") %>% pull(locus_tag)

hits <- sum(bcaa %in% down)   # pathway genes that are down

# P(at least `hits` pathway genes among the down genes, drawn at random from the universe)
p <- phyper(hits - 1, length(bcaa), length(universe) - length(bcaa), length(down),
            lower.tail = FALSE)
cat(hits, "of", length(bcaa), "pathway genes are down; expected by chance:",
    round(length(bcaa) * length(down) / length(universe), 1), "; p =", signif(p, 2), "\n")
```
7 of the 11 genes of the pathway are down, where less than 1 was expected: p < 10⁻⁸. Check with Fisher's test: `fisher.test(table(universe %in% bcaa, universe %in% down), alternative = "greater")`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_ora
#| check: true
bcaa <- pathway_genes %>% filter(pathway == "ko00290") %>% pull(locus_tag)
expected <- fisher.test(table(universe %in% bcaa, universe %in% down), alternative = "greater")$p.value
ok <- is.numeric(hits) && hits == sum(bcaa %in% down) && isTRUE(all.equal(p, expected))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct, and identical to Fisher's exact test. Branched-chain amino acid synthesis is switched down in LPS mice.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: hits is the number of pathway genes (bcaa) that are also in down.")
}
```

### All pathways at once

The same test for every pathway with at least 10 genes. Since we run many tests, we adjust the p-values for multiple testing (Benjamini–Hochberg):

```{webr}
ora <- function(selected) {
  pathway_genes %>%
    group_by(pathway) %>%
    summarise(size = n(), hits = sum(locus_tag %in% selected)) %>%
    filter(size >= 10) %>%
    mutate(
      expected = size * length(selected) / length(universe),
      ratio = hits / expected,
      p = phyper(hits - 1, size, length(universe) - size, length(selected), lower.tail = FALSE),
      padj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")
    ) %>%
    left_join(pathway_names, by = "pathway") %>%
    arrange(p) %>%
    select(pathway, name, size, hits, expected, ratio, padj)
}

ora(down) %>% head(8)
ora(up) %>% head(8)
```

Amino acid biosynthesis pathways stand out among the genes switched down in LPS mice. No pathway passes the adjusted cut-off for the up-regulated genes: they are spread over many functions, or not in KEGG pathways at all.

When you read such a table, look at more than the p-value: the **ratio** of hits to expected hits says how strong the enrichment is, and a pathway with only one or two hits is weak evidence, however small its p-value. A common rule of thumb is to require at least 3 hits.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Choose the universe carefully
Using all genes of the genome as the universe, instead of the genes that were tested and annotated, inflates the significance: unannotated genes can never be hits.
:::

## Gene set enrichment analysis

ORA needs a cut-off (here: adjusted p < 0.01 and a fold change above 2), and ignores everything below it. **GSEA** uses all genes instead. It ranks them and asks whether a pathway's genes cluster at the top or the bottom of the ranking.

We rank genes by DESeq2's **Wald statistic** (`stat`): the fold change divided by its standard error. Ranking by the fold change itself would put lowly expressed genes, whose fold changes are large but noisy, at the extremes. We use the fast implementation in `fgsea`:

```{webr}
library(fgsea)

ranks <- i48 %>%
  filter(locus_tag %in% universe) %>%
  arrange(desc(stat)) %>%
  { setNames(.$stat, .$locus_tag) }

set.seed(42)
gsea <- fgsea(split(pathway_genes$locus_tag, pathway_genes$pathway), ranks,
              minSize = 10, maxSize = 500,
              BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam(progressbar = FALSE))

gsea %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  left_join(pathway_names, by = "pathway") %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(NES) %>%
  select(pathway, name, size, NES, padj)
```

The **normalised enrichment score** (NES) is negative for pathways whose genes are mostly down in LPS mice, and positive for pathways mostly up. Down in LPS: amino acid biosynthesis, as with ORA, and **Ribosome**, which ORA missed: its genes go down together, but only 1 of its 53 genes passes the ORA cut-off. In Part 2, I48's drop in ribosomal protein transcripts was only a trend (p ≈ 0.09); GSEA, which tests the ribosome genes' ranks together, gives stronger evidence. Up in LPS: ABC transporters.

```{webr}
plotEnrichment(split(pathway_genes$locus_tag, pathway_genes$pathway)[["ko03010"]], ranks) +
  labs(title = "Ribosome (ko03010) in I48", x = "Gene rank (most up in LPS → most down)", y = "Enrichment score")
```

Each vertical line is a ribosome gene in the ranking. They pile up at the right end, among the genes most strongly down in LPS mice.

## STRING: how do the genes work together?

[STRING](https://string-db.org) collects known and predicted interactions between proteins. It knows the I48 genome by its locus tags. Print the down-regulated genes:

```{webr}
down_all <- i48 %>% filter(padj < 0.01, log2FoldChange < -1) %>% pull(locus_tag)
writeLines(down_all)
```

Copy the list, open [string-db.org](https://string-db.org), choose **Multiple proteins**, paste the list, enter *Bacteroides caecimuris* as the organism, and press **Search**. Genes that are connected in the network often work together, such as the enzymes of one pathway, or the subunits of a transporter.

## Running this on your own computer

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## GO enrichment with topGO, and clusterProfiler
In R on your own computer, you can also test Gene Ontology (GO) terms with [topGO](https://bioconductor.org/packages/topGO/), and run ORA and GSEA with [clusterProfiler](https://bioconductor.org/packages/clusterProfiler/), which also makes many plots. Both need the GO.db annotation package, which doesn't run in a browser.

```{.r .notest}
library(clusterProfiler)

# the same ORA as above
enricher(down, universe = universe, TERM2GENE = pathway_genes[, c("pathway", "locus_tag")],
         pvalueCutoff = 0.05, minGSSize = 10)

# GO terms with topGO: gene2go is a named list of GO IDs per locus tag (e.g. from eggNOG-mapper)
library(topGO)
scores <- setNames(i48$padj, i48$locus_tag)
go_data <- new("topGOdata", ontology = "BP", allGenes = scores,
               geneSel = function(p) p < 0.01, nodeSize = 10,
               annot = annFUN.gene2GO, gene2GO = gene2go)
GenTable(go_data, weight01 = runTest(go_data, algorithm = "weight01", statistic = "fisher"), topNodes = 20)
```
:::

## Check yourself

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("A pathway has 3 of its 10 genes among your down-regulated genes, with an adjusted p-value of 0.4. What do you conclude?", [
  {text: "The pathway is not affected", correct: false, why: "Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence: with few genes, ORA has little power. GSEA, or a closer look at the genes, may tell more."},
  {text: "There's no evidence that the pathway is over-represented", correct: true, why: "That's all a non-significant test says. Small pathways rarely reach significance."},
  {text: "The pathway is switched down", correct: false, why: "3 of 10 could easily happen by chance, given how many genes are down overall."}
])
```

## Key points

- **ORA** tests whether a pathway has more responding genes than expected; it needs a cut-off and a well-chosen **universe**.
- **GSEA** uses the whole ranking, and finds pathways whose genes shift together, even by small amounts.
- In I48, inflammation of the host switches down **ribosomes** and **amino acid biosynthesis**. That's consistent with slower growth, but other explanations are possible: a sick host eats less, which changes the bacteria's food supply.
- Enrichment can only see annotated genes; in bacteria, that's often less than half of them.
